title: Remember and Observe in One Word
hookLine: Shabbat can be kept fully, partly, or through one practice; choose honestly
carry: remember and observe, spoken as one
tomorrow: a sage salted the fish himself on Fridays. why not let someone else?

cards: Friday afternoons tend to end in a pileup: the last emails, the last errands, the group chat making plans. Into that, the Torah drops a command, and then drops it again in different words.
In Exodus: "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." In Deuteronomy: "Observe the sabbath day, to keep it holy." Remember, or observe?
The sages' answer is that God said both at once, in a single breath.

teach.b: The Talmud says remember and observe were spoken as one word, something no human mouth could say or ear could hear. The Friday-night song Lecha Dodi sings it: shamor v'zachor, observe and remember, in one utterance.
Two words, two halves of the day.
Zachor, remember, is the doing: candles, a cup of wine, bread on the table, a song.
Shamor, observe, is the guarding: setting work down and letting the week stop. For Orthodox Jews, the full laws of Shabbat are binding, not a menu.
Other Jewish movements teach that a person can grow into it, one practice at a time. This lesson ranks no one.

It asks something simpler: where do you honestly begin? Fully, partly, or with a single practice, as long as both words get a share: one thing you do to remember, one thing you set down to keep. Some begin with candles.
The one lighting them draws the light in with their hands, covers their eyes, says the blessing, then opens them on the flame.
Something to tell a friend tonight: the sages say the two Shabbat commands were spoken in one word.

how: Orthodox Jews keep the full laws of Shabbat from Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall; Conservative, Reform, Reconstructionist and secular Jews keep it in a range of ways, often beginning with candles, kiddush over wine, challah and a family meal, and sometimes a set time without work or screens.

games.q: your partner grew up keeping a full Shabbat; you grew up with none. you're planning your first one together. what does 'choose your Shabbat' suggest?
o: take on their full Shabbat on day one, or it doesn't count.
choose honestly where to begin: one thing to remember, one thing to set down.
skip it until the two of you agree on everything.
games.why: both words get a share: something done to remember, something set down to keep. where you begin can grow; honesty is the point.

practice: Find a small light: a candle if it's safe to light one, or a lamp, or a dimmed screen. Draw your hands toward you around it, then cover your eyes and stay there for a few slow breaths, feeling the warmth or just the dark.
Open your eyes on the light, and name two things to yourself: one you'll do to remember Shabbat, one you'll set down to keep it.

wordCard.voice: Choose your Shabbat: deciding honestly how you'll keep it, fully, partly or through one practice, with something remembered and something set down.

orig.note: Hebrew: observe and remember, the two Shabbat words, sung together in Lecha Dodi.

carryVoice: Keep this one: remember and observe, spoken as one. One thing to do, one thing to set down, chosen honestly.
